prompt: my 14 year old got tackled at football practice and now his collarbone area is poking up weird is that broken
response: Yes, a visible bump or deformity over the collarbone after a hard impact is a classic sign of a clavicle fracture (broken collarbone). The bone has likely broken and the pieces are now overlapping or pushing upward, creating that "poking up" appearance.  He needs to be seen by a doctor for an X-ray to confirm the break and determine its severity. In the meantime, you can help manage his pain by immobilizing his arm in a sling—a scarf or triangular piece of cloth will work—and applying a cold pack to the area for 15-20 minutes. You can also give him an over-the-counter pain reliever like ibuprofen or paracetamol.  Go to an emergency department if he has any numbness or tingling in his arm or hand, if his hand feels cold, or if the skin over the bump is broken or stretched very thin.

prompt: I was chopping onions and the knife slipped and cut the tip of my finger pretty deep theres a flap of skin hanging off what do I do
response: First, apply firm, direct pressure to the cut with a clean cloth or gauze to stop the bleeding. After the bleeding slows, gently wash the wound with cool, clean water and mild soap. Do not try to cut off the flap of skin; gently place it back over the wound, as it can help with healing. Apply an antibiotic ointment and cover the cut with a clean bandage.  You should go to a hospital or urgent care clinic if the bleeding does not stop after 15 minutes of pressure, if the cut is very deep and gaping open, or if you cannot feel or move the tip of your finger. Also, watch for signs of infection over the next few days, such as increasing redness, swelling, pus, or a fever. If you haven't had a tetanus shot in the last 5-10 years, you may need a booster.

prompt: I have this throbbing toothache and now the gum around it is swollen and there's a bump with pus should I go to the ER or a dentist

They will likely want to check your thyroid hormone levels (TSH, T4, T3) to see what is happening and adjust your medication if needed. You should not change your medication dose on your own. If you experience a very fast or irregular heartbeat, chest pain, or severe shortness of breath, you should seek emergency medical care immediately.

Avoid holding the baby close to the affected area, and do not share towels or bedding. The risk of spreading the virus is gone once the rash has completely crusted over. For your severe pain, see a doctor as soon as possible, as antiviral medication can help reduce the severity and length of the illness.

prompt: every time I stand up quickly I see stars and nearly black out and my blood pressure sitting is fine but when I stand it drops to like 80 over 50
response: This is a classic sign of orthostatic hypotension, which is a drop in blood pressure when you stand up. When you stand, gravity pulls blood down into your legs, and for a moment, not enough blood gets to your brain, causing the dizziness and vision changes. The most important thing you can do is to stand up slowly, giving your body time to adjust. Sit on the edge of your bed or chair for a minute before you stand up completely.  Staying well-hydrated by drinking plenty of water is also very important, as dehydration can make this much worse. Before you stand, try pumping your ankles or clenching your leg muscles to help push blood back up toward your heart. If you ever actually faint and fall, if it is accompanied by chest pain, or if this is a new or worsening problem, you should see a doctor to check for any underlying causes.

To deal with this, the single most important thing they can do is stand up *slowly*. Make sure to drink plenty of water, as dehydration is a major contributor. If they actually lose consciousness, experience chest pain, or the problem is new or worsening, it's time to see a doctor to rule out any underlying causes.
